analysis.one_liner: Imposes a one-time 14.25% federal tax on personal net worth above $10 million.
analysis.headline: The bill sits in the House Ways and Means Committee with zero cosponsors and no action since its April referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would impose a one-time tax of 14.25% on every dollar of net worth above $10 million, measured on the day the bill became law. Primary homes and the mortgages on them would be excluded from the calculation, and trusts that benefit U.S. citizens or residents would be covered. The bill's stated purpose is paying down the national debt, and it is built around a wealth tax plan Donald Trump proposed as a presidential candidate in 1999.
analysis.who_benefits: The main beneficiary is the federal treasury, which would collect an estimated large one-time sum from households with more than $10 million in net worth; the bill's findings argue the money would reduce the national debt that future taxpayers, including today's workers and their children, otherwise carry. Ordinary taxpayers owe nothing under the tax, since net worth below $10 million is exempt and the family home is excluded.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a one-time 14.25% tax on net worth above $10 million, so households below that threshold owe nothing.
Excludes the taxpayer's principal residence and the debt owed on it from net worth, protecting the main asset most families have.
The bill's findings cite an estimate that a similar tax would raise $5.7 trillion and lower the debt-to-GDP ratio from about 101% to 83%, reducing the burden passed to future generations.
Covers trusts whose beneficiaries are U.S. citizens or residents, so wealth held in trust cannot simply escape the tax.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals, and certain trusts, whose net worth (excluding their home) exceeds $10 million on the enactment date, who would owe 14.25% of the excess as a one-time charge. That is roughly the wealthiest 1-2% of households.

drawbacks.text: The $5.7 trillion revenue figure in the bill's findings is Donald Trump's own 1999 estimate for his proposed tax, not a current, independent score of this bill's actual yield.

Measuring the fair market value of every asset a wealthy person owns on a single date is difficult and would invite disputes, appraisal fights, and years of litigation over what counts toward net worth.
A one-time tax of this size could force large holders to sell assets quickly to raise cash, which could disturb markets and hurt ordinary investors' retirement accounts.
Excluding the principal residence creates a ready avoidance path: shifting wealth into homes and mortgage paydowns would reduce taxable net worth, weakening the tax and adding complexity.
Because it is a one-time tax, it generates no continuing revenue stream for ongoing programs; its entire benefit is a one-time reduction of debt.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If enacted as written, the bill would place a large one-time charge on the wealthiest households and use it to reduce federal debt, a benefit that is real but diffuse and spread over future generations, while the costs fall on a small, concentrated group. The honest caveats are that the headline revenue number is a decades-old estimate rather than a current score, that valuing every asset on one date would be contentious, and that the primary-residence exemption invites avoidance. The bill also carries a pointed name and findings section quoting Donald Trump and other conservatives on the debt, signaling its political purpose alongside its fiscal one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action on it; it has no cosponsors, so nothing further has happened.

narrative.text: Rep. Juan Vargas introduced the bill on April 15, 2026, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
No other action has been taken on the bill since that referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost anything from this bill except in anticipation: the wealthiest households, who would owe the tax if it passed, are better off that it has not moved, while everyone else's position is unchanged because the tax has never been enacted or voted on.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthiest households, spared the tax so far

for.name: Rep. Juan Vargas
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means, building it around Donald Trump's 1999 wealth tax proposal.

against.name: Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since its April 15 referral; no hearing, markup, or floor consideration has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have been held and the bill has zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split has formed; it rests with a single Democratic sponsor in a Republican-controlled House.

industries.industry: Wealthiest households (net worth above $10 million) and family trusts
industries.note: The bill would charge them 14.25% of net worth above $10 million, measured on one date, with the family home excluded. Their interest is in keeping the tax from ever becoming law, while the bill's stated benefit, debt reduction, accrues to the general public.

analysis.trajectory: With no cosponsors, no committee action more than a month after referral, and a House majority unlikely to bring a tax on large fortunes to the floor, the bill is all but certain to die in committee when this Congress ends in January 2027. Its realistic function is as a statement piece quoting the President's own 1999 debt-reduction proposal.
